title: Postcomposition by an isogeny multiplies degree extended by zero
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure] and let $A,B,C$ be abelian varieties over $k$ [def-sc-abelian-variety] of the same dimension $g\geq1$ [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. Let $h:A\to B$ and $u:B\to C$ be group-scheme homomorphisms [def-sc-group-scheme], with $u$ an isogeny [def-sc-isogeny]. For a homomorphism $f$ between these varieties define $d(f)$ to be the order of its scheme-theoretic kernel when $f$ is an isogeny, and $0$ otherwise. Then $u\circ h$ is an isogeny if and only if $h$ is an isogeny, and
$$d(u\circ h)=(\deg u)d(h).$$
No separability assumption is imposed on $u$ or $h$.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 7.1 and the identification of degree with function-field degree, printed p.32; multiplicativity in Remark 8.6, printed p.36. The tower formula is Stacks Project, Morphisms, Tag 02NZ, lemma-degree-composition, in literature/stacks-project/morphisms.tex; the zero case uses the finite map on the closed image.

proof.text: Suppose $h$ is an isogeny. By [def-sc-isogeny], both $h$ and $u$ are surjective. For every point $c$ of $C$, choose $b$ over $c$ under $u$ and then $a$ over $b$ under $h$; hence $u\circ h$ is surjective. It is a group-scheme homomorphism, since composition preserves the multiplication compatibility diagrams in [def-sc-group-scheme]. Apply [lem-sfb-equal-dimension-isogeny-criterion] to $A,C$, whose dimensions both equal $g$, to conclude that $u\circ h$ is an isogeny.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 8.6, printed p.36. Finite-map cancellation and constant finite locally free rank multiplication make the composite and zero cases explicit.

proof.text: Conversely suppose $u\circ h$ is an isogeny. By [lem-sc-isogeny-degree], $u$ and $u\circ h$ are finite. A finite morphism is separated, as recorded in [lem-weil-pbc-finite-permanence-over-separated]; apply that node to $h$ followed by $u$ to deduce that $h$ is finite. The scheme-theoretic kernel $\ker h=A\times_{B,h,e_B}\operatorname{Spec}k$ is the base change of $h$ along the identity section, by [def-sc-group-scheme]. Finiteness is preserved by arbitrary base change by [lem-trf-finite-radicial-basechange], so this kernel is finite over $k$. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-kernel-equal-dimension-isogeny] to $h$: the field is algebraically closed, $A,B$ are abelian varieties, their dimensions agree (the topological Krull dimensions of the statement equal the local-ring dimensions of [def-pc-dimension] by [lem-pc-scheme-dimension-local-rings]), and the kernel has just been proved finite. Thus $h$ is surjective, and together with its finite kernel this makes it an isogeny by [def-sc-isogeny].

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 8.6, printed p.36. Finite-map cancellation and constant finite locally free rank multiplication make the composite and zero cases explicit.

proof.text: Assume $h$ is an isogeny, so step 1 makes $v=u\circ h$ an isogeny too. For each of $h,u,v$, [lem-sc-isogeny-degree] identifies the kernel order with the constant rank of its structure-sheaf pushforward, hence its finite-flat degree. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-kernel-equal-dimension-isogeny] to each map to obtain finite local freeness: all source and target dimensions are $g$, also in the sense of [def-pc-dimension] by [lem-pc-scheme-dimension-local-rings], and all three kernels are finite. In the fibre-degree convention [def-pc-finite-locally-free], their degrees are therefore $d(h),\deg u,d(v)$ respectively. Apply [lem-sfb-finite-locally-free-degree-composition] to $h$ followed by $u$: $v$ has constant degree $d(h)\deg u$. Compare this with its degree $d(v)$ at the identity point $e_C:\operatorname{Spec}k\to C$, which exists by [def-sc-group-scheme]. This yields $d(u\circ h)=d(h)\deg u=(\deg u)d(h)$. All kernel orders and fibre degrees are algebra dimensions; no point counting or separability is used.

source.place: Chapter I, Proposition 7.1 and following degree paragraph, printed p.32; Remark 8.6, printed p.36. Finite-map cancellation and constant finite locally free rank multiplication make the composite and zero cases explicit.

proof.text: If $h$ is not an isogeny, step 2 shows by contrapositive that $u\circ h$ is not an isogeny. The definition of $d$ in the statement then gives $d(h)=d(u\circ h)=0$, so $d(u\circ h)=0=(\deg u)d(h)$. Together with steps 1 and 3 this proves the equivalence and the formula in all cases.
